description: Discrete and continuous transforms, convolution and correlation, digital filter design and application, spectral estimation and wavelet analysis. These functions operate on numeric lists, images, TimeSeries and Audio objects alike.

tools.name: Fourier
tools.description: Computes the discrete Fourier transform of a list or array using an FFT algorithm. The default convention includes a 1/Sqrt[n] normalization, which FourierParameters can change to match other conventions. It works in any number of dimensions.

parameters.name: FourierParameters
parameters.description: {a, b} convention; {-1, 1} gives the usual signal-processing convention.

tools.example:
data = Table[Sin[2 Pi 5 t] + 0.5 Sin[2 Pi 12 t], {t, 0, 1 - 1/256, 1/256}];
ListLinePlot[Abs[Fourier[data]][[1 ;; 40]]]
tools.notes: Fourier is 1-indexed, so the zero-frequency term is the first element. Use RotateRight or Fourier on shifted data for centered spectra.

tools.name: InverseFourier
tools.description: Computes the inverse discrete Fourier transform, reconstructing a signal from its spectrum. It uses the same FourierParameters convention as Fourier, so the two invert each other exactly. Use it after spectral filtering to return to the time domain.

tools.name: FourierDCT
tools.description: Computes the discrete cosine transform of real data, with four standard variants selected by a type number. DCT-II is the basis of JPEG compression and gives good energy compaction for smooth signals. It avoids the complex arithmetic of a full DFT.
tools.notes: FourierDCT[list, 3] is the inverse of FourierDCT[list, 2] up to scaling.

tools.name: FourierDST
tools.description: Computes the discrete sine transform of real data, in one of four variants. It is the natural transform for problems with zero boundary conditions, such as vibrating strings and Dirichlet PDEs. It complements FourierDCT.
tools.example:
data = Table[Sin[Pi n/32], {n, 1, 31}];
FourierDST[data, 1] // Chop // Short

tools.name: FourierSequenceTransform
tools.description: Computes the discrete-time Fourier transform of a sequence, giving a function of the continuous frequency variable. It is the symbolic tool for analyzing discrete-time systems. InverseFourierSequenceTransform recovers the sequence.
tools.example: FourierSequenceTransform[(1/2)^n UnitStep[n], n, w]

tools.name: ListConvolve
tools.description: Convolves a kernel with a list, with control over alignment and boundary treatment via overhang parameters and cyclic padding. It underlies FIR filtering and moving-window operations on sequences. Multi-dimensional arrays are supported.
tools.usage:
ListConvolve[kernel, list]
ListConvolve[kernel, list, k]
ListConvolve[kernel, list, {kL, kR}, padding]
tools.notes: ListConvolve reverses the kernel; ListCorrelate does not, which matters for asymmetric kernels.

tools.name: ListCorrelate
tools.description: Correlates a kernel with a list without reversing the kernel, giving sliding dot products. It is the natural operation for template matching and moving statistics. Overhang and padding arguments match ListConvolve.
tools.usage:
ListCorrelate[kernel, list]
ListCorrelate[kernel, list, {kL, kR}, padding]
tools.example:
signal = Join[ConstantArray[0, 20], {1, 2, 3, 2, 1}, ConstantArray[0, 20]];
ListLinePlot[ListCorrelate[{1, 2, 3, 2, 1}, signal]]

tools.name: LowpassFilter
tools.description: Applies a lowpass FIR filter with a given cutoff frequency to data, an audio object or an image. The cutoff is in radians per sample unless a sample rate is supplied. Filter order and window function are configurable.
tools.usage:
LowpassFilter[data, wc]
LowpassFilter[data, wc, n]
LowpassFilter[data, wc, n, window]
tools.example:
data = Table[Sin[2 Pi 3 t] + 0.4 Sin[2 Pi 40 t], {t, 0, 2, 1/500}];
ListLinePlot[{data, LowpassFilter[data, 2 Pi 10/500, 60]}, PlotRange -> All]
tools.notes: Pass a Quantity cutoff together with sampled audio to work directly in hertz.

tools.name: HighpassFilter
tools.description: Applies a highpass FIR filter that removes slow trends and low-frequency content below a cutoff. It is the standard way to detrend a signal or emphasize transients. Order and window control the transition sharpness and ripple.
tools.example:
data = Table[t/5 + Sin[2 Pi 20 t], {t, 0, 2, 1/500}];
ListLinePlot[HighpassFilter[data, 2 Pi 5/500, 80]]

tools.name: BandpassFilter
tools.description: Keeps only the frequency content between two cutoffs, attenuating everything outside the band. It is the main tool for isolating a frequency band of interest in a signal. Cutoffs can be given as plain numbers or as Quantity frequencies.
tools.example:
data = Table[Sin[2 Pi 5 t] + Sin[2 Pi 50 t] + Sin[2 Pi 120 t], {t, 0, 1, 1/1000}];
ListLinePlot[BandpassFilter[data, {2 Pi 40/1000, 2 Pi 60/1000}, 120]]

tools.name: BandstopFilter
tools.description: Removes the frequency content inside a band while passing everything outside it, the classic notch filter. It is used to suppress mains hum and other narrowband interference. Order and window control the depth and width of the notch.
tools.example:
data = Table[Sin[2 Pi 3 t] + 0.5 Sin[2 Pi 50 t], {t, 0, 2, 1/1000}];
ListLinePlot[BandstopFilter[data, {2 Pi 45/1000, 2 Pi 55/1000}, 200]]

tools.name: LeastSquaresFilterKernel
tools.description: Computes the FIR filter kernel that best approximates an ideal frequency response in the least-squares sense. Returning the kernel rather than filtered data lets you inspect, plot or reuse the filter. Apply it with ListConvolve.
tools.example:
k = LeastSquaresFilterKernel[Pi/4, 41];
ListLinePlot[k, Filling -> Axis]
tools.notes: Related kernel constructors include HammingWindow-shaped designs and the various *FilterModel functions for IIR designs.

tools.name: ButterworthFilterModel
tools.description: Creates a maximally flat Butterworth analog or digital filter model of given order and cutoff. The result is a TransferFunctionModel that can be analyzed with BodePlot or converted with ToDiscreteTimeModel. Use it when passband flatness matters more than roll-off sharpness.
tools.example:
tf = ButterworthFilterModel[{5, 2 Pi 100}];
BodePlot[tf, GridLines -> Automatic]

tools.name: Chebyshev1FilterModel
tools.description: Creates a Chebyshev type I filter model, which allows ripple in the passband in exchange for a steeper transition than Butterworth. Order and allowed ripple are specified. Use it when a sharp cutoff matters more than flat passband gain.
tools.example:
tf = Chebyshev1FilterModel[{6, 1}, 0.5];
BodePlot[tf]
tools.notes: Chebyshev2FilterModel puts the ripple in the stopband instead; EllipticFilterModel ripples in both and is the sharpest.

tools.name: Chebyshev2FilterModel
tools.description: Creates a Chebyshev type II (inverse Chebyshev) filter with a flat passband and equiripple stopband. It gives a sharper roll-off than Butterworth without passband ripple. Use it when passband fidelity and good stopband rejection are both needed.
tools.example: BodePlot[Chebyshev2FilterModel[{6, 1}, 40]]

tools.name: EllipticFilterModel
tools.description: Creates an elliptic (Cauer) filter, which achieves the steepest possible transition for a given order by allowing ripple in both bands. It is the most efficient choice when order must be kept low. Passband and stopband ripple are both specified.
tools.example: BodePlot[EllipticFilterModel[{5, 1}, {0.5, 50}]]

tools.name: BesselFilterModel
tools.description: Creates a Bessel filter, which has maximally flat group delay and therefore minimal waveform distortion. Its amplitude roll-off is gentler than other designs of the same order. Use it when preserving pulse shape matters, as in data transmission.
tools.example: BodePlot[BesselFilterModel[{6, 1}]]

tools.name: Periodogram
tools.description: Plots the power spectral density estimate of a signal, in decibels by default. It accepts lists, TimeSeries and Audio objects, and handles windowing and averaging. Use it as the primary tool for finding periodic components.
tools.usage:
Periodogram[data]
Periodogram[data, n, d, window, opts]

parameters.name: SampleRate
parameters.description: Sample rate so the frequency axis is in hertz.

parameters.name: window
parameters.description: Smoothing window such as HannWindow or BlackmanWindow.

tools.notes: PeriodogramArray returns the numeric values instead of a plot.

tools.name: PeriodogramArray
tools.description: Returns the numeric power spectral density of a signal as an array rather than a plot. Partitioning and windowing parameters match Periodogram. Use it when you need the spectrum for further computation.

tools.name: Spectrogram
tools.description: Plots how the frequency content of a signal evolves over time, as a short-time Fourier transform image. Window size, offset and window function control the time-frequency trade-off. Use it for speech, music and any non-stationary signal.
tools.usage:
Spectrogram[data]
Spectrogram[data, n, d, window, opts]
tools.example:
chirp = Table[Sin[2 Pi (5 + 40 t) t], {t, 0, 4, 1/1000}];
Spectrogram[chirp, 256, 32, SampleRate -> 1000]
tools.notes: SpectrogramArray returns the underlying complex or magnitude array.

tools.name: SpectrogramArray
tools.description: Computes the short-time Fourier transform of a signal and returns it as a numeric array of complex coefficients. It is the computational core behind Spectrogram. Use it for time-frequency feature extraction and spectral editing.
tools.notes: ShortTimeFourier returns a structured object with metadata and supports inversion via InverseShortTimeFourier.

tools.name: ShortTimeFourier
tools.description: Computes the short-time Fourier transform and returns a ShortTimeFourierData object carrying the coefficients together with window and sample-rate metadata. This makes round-tripping through InverseShortTimeFourier reliable. Use it for spectral modification and resynthesis.

tools.name: DiscreteWaveletTransform
tools.description: Computes a discrete wavelet transform of data using a specified wavelet family and refinement level. The result is a DiscreteWaveletData object whose coefficients can be extracted, thresholded and inverted. Use it for multiresolution analysis, denoising and compression.
tools.notes: StationaryWaveletTransform is shift-invariant and often better for denoising; InverseWaveletTransform reconstructs.

tools.name: ContinuousWaveletTransform
tools.description: Computes a continuous wavelet transform over a range of scales, giving a fine time-scale picture of the signal. It is well suited to detecting transients and instantaneous frequency. The result plots naturally as a scalogram.

tools.name: InverseWaveletTransform
tools.description: Reconstructs a signal from wavelet data, optionally using only a chosen subset of coefficient bands. Zeroing or thresholding coefficients before inversion performs denoising or band selection. It works with both discrete and stationary wavelet data.

tools.name: WaveletScalogram
tools.description: Plots wavelet coefficients as a time-scale image, the wavelet counterpart of a spectrogram. Larger scales appear as broader, lower-frequency structures. Use it to localize transients in time and scale simultaneously.

tools.name: WaveletListPlot
tools.description: Plots the coefficient sequences of each wavelet band on separate aligned axes. It makes the multiresolution decomposition of a signal easy to read band by band. Use it to decide which bands carry signal and which carry noise.
tools.notes: WaveletMatrixPlot shows the same information as a stacked image.

tools.name: WaveletMatrixPlot
tools.description: Displays wavelet coefficients as a matrix image with bands laid out hierarchically. For 2D transforms it shows the familiar quadrant decomposition of an image. Use it for a compact overview of the whole coefficient set.
tools.example:
img = ExampleData[{"TestImage", "Lena"}];
WaveletMatrixPlot[DiscreteWaveletTransform[img, HaarWavelet[], 2]]

tools.name: Upsample
tools.description: Increases the sample rate of a list or array by inserting zeros (or a given value) between samples. It is the first half of an interpolation chain, usually followed by a lowpass filter. Multi-dimensional data is supported.
tools.example:
data = {1, 2, 3, 4};
Upsample[data, 3]
tools.notes: Downsample keeps every n-th sample; ArrayResample performs full resampling with interpolation.

tools.name: Downsample
tools.description: Keeps every n-th element of a list or array, reducing the sample rate. Apply an anti-alias lowpass filter first to avoid aliasing. An offset selects which phase of the samples is kept.
tools.example:
data = Table[Sin[2 Pi 3 t], {t, 0, 1, 1/100}];
ListLinePlot[Downsample[LowpassFilter[data, Pi/4], 4]]

tools.name: ArrayResample
tools.description: Resamples an array to a new size using a chosen interpolation method, handling arbitrary non-integer ratios. It is the general-purpose resizing function for numeric data. Use it for grid conversion and rate change.
tools.example:
data = Table[Sin[2 Pi t], {t, 0, 1, 1/50}];
ListLinePlot[ArrayResample[data, 200, Resampling -> "Cubic"]]

tools.name: SavitzkyGolayMatrix
tools.description: Generates a Savitzky-Golay smoothing or differentiating kernel that fits a local polynomial to a sliding window. It smooths data while preserving peak height and width much better than a moving average. Apply the kernel with ListConvolve.

tools.name: HilbertFilter
tools.description: Applies a Hilbert transform filter, shifting every frequency component by 90 degrees. Combining the result with the original gives the analytic signal, from which envelope and instantaneous phase follow. Use it for demodulation and envelope detection.

tools.name: DifferentiatorFilter
tools.description: Applies an FIR filter that approximates differentiation, giving the derivative of a sampled signal with controlled noise amplification. Order and window control the bandwidth over which the approximation holds. Use it instead of naive differencing on noisy data.
tools.example:
data = Table[Sin[2 Pi 2 t], {t, 0, 1, 1/200}];
ListLinePlot[DifferentiatorFilter[data, 60]]

tools.name: CorrelationFunction
tools.description: Computes the autocorrelation or cross-correlation of data or of a stochastic process at given lags. Peaks in the autocorrelation reveal periodicity and characteristic timescales. It works on lists, TimeSeries and symbolic processes.
tools.example:
data = Table[Sin[2 Pi t/10] + RandomReal[{-0.5, 0.5}], {t, 200}];
ListLinePlot[CorrelationFunction[data, {30}], Filling -> Axis]
tools.notes: PowerSpectralDensity gives the frequency-domain counterpart for processes and data.

tools.name: PowerSpectralDensity
tools.description: Gives the power spectral density of a time series or a symbolic random process as a function of frequency. For processes it returns a closed-form expression, and for data it estimates the spectrum. Use it to characterize noise color and resonances.
tools.example:
PowerSpectralDensity[ARProcess[{0.5}, 1], w]
Plot[Evaluate[%], {w, 0, Pi}]
